The router sends its whole table to every neighbour
The route is marked unreachable: metric set to 16
The route, still advertised with metric 16 meanwhile, is deleted
At once, at most one every 1–5 s
Changed routes are sent without waiting for the 30 s timer

concepts.text:
Worked example 1: RIP update processing at router R (each hop adds 1)
R's table before:  Net1 2 via A | Net2 5 via B | Net3 3 via C
Update from B:     Net1 1 | Net2 7 | Net3 1 | Net4 14
Add one hop:       Net1 2 | Net2 8 | Net3 2 | Net4 15
Net1: 2 via B is not better than 2 via A -> keep 2 via A
Net2: B is the current next hop -> accept 8 via B although it is worse
Net3: 2 via B is better than 3 via C -> replace with 2 via B
Net4: new and 15 < 16 -> add 15 via B (one hop more would be unreachable)
R's table after:   Net1 2 via A | Net2 8 via B | Net3 2 via B | Net4 15 via B
OSPF router roles and the main LSA (link state advertisement) types:
items: Internal router: all interfaces in one area. Backbone router: at least one interface in area 0.
Area border router (ABR): joins an area to area 0 and summarises routes between them. Autonomous system boundary router (ASBR): brings in routes from outside OSPF, such as BGP or static routes.
Type 1 router LSA: every router describes its own links; flooded only inside its area.
Type 2 network LSA: the designated router describes a multi-access network and the routers attached to it.
Type 3 summary LSA: an ABR advertises one area's networks into another; type 4 tells other areas how to reach an ASBR.
Type 5 AS-external LSA: an ASBR advertises external routes to the whole OSPF domain except stub areas; type 7 carries them inside a not-so-stubby area (NSSA).
Hello packets every 10 s (dead interval 40 s) on broadcast links find and keep neighbours; two routers become neighbours only if area ID, hello/dead timers and authentication match.

concepts.text: On a shared segment with n routers, an adjacency between every pair would need n(n − 1)/2 adjacencies and would flood the same LSAs many times. OSPF therefore elects a designated router (DR) and a backup designated router (BDR): the highest interface priority wins (default 1, and 0 means never eligible), and a tie is broken by the highest router ID. Every other router (a DROther) forms full adjacencies only with the DR and BDR, sends its updates to 224.0.0.6, and the DR floods them to everyone on 224.0.0.5. The election is not pre-emptive, so a higher-priority router that joins later does not take over until the DR fails.

concepts.plainText: Adjacencies on a segment of n routers: full mesh n(n − 1)/2; with DR and BDR 2(n − 2) + 1 = 2n − 3 (for n = 6: 15 against 9)

concepts.text:
Worked example 2: OSPF cost = reference / bandwidth, fraction dropped, minimum 1
Path P1: two 1 Gbps links        Path P2: one 100 Mbps link
Reference 10^8 (100 Mbps, the old default):
  1 Gbps -> 0.1 -> raised to 1;  100 Mbps -> 1
  P1 = 1 + 1 = 2,  P2 = 1        -> OSPF picks P2, the slower path
Reference 10^10 (10 Gbps):
  1 Gbps -> 10;  100 Mbps -> 100
  P1 = 10 + 10 = 20,  P2 = 100   -> OSPF picks P1
Rule: configure the same reference, at least the fastest link speed, on every router

Worked example 3: BGP routes to 203.0.113.0/24, originated by AS 300
Router in AS 100 hears:   via AS 200: AS_PATH 200 300
                          via AS 400: AS_PATH 400 500 300
No local policy: equal LOCAL_PREF, shorter AS_PATH wins -> via AS 200
Import policy sets LOCAL_PREF 200 on routes from AS 400 (others 100):
  LOCAL_PREF is compared before AS_PATH length -> via AS 400
To its eBGP peers AS 100 advertises AS_PATH 100 400 500 300 (own AS prepended)
To its iBGP peers inside AS 100 the AS_PATH stays 400 500 300
A router in AS 500 that hears 100 400 500 300 finds 500 in it and drops it (loop)
Multicast details beyond the basic page:
items: IGMP (IP protocol 2, TTL 1) works only on the local network: the router sends General Queries (every 125 s by default) and hosts answer with Membership Reports; IGMPv2 added Leave Group, and IGMPv3 lets a host name the sources it wants (source-specific multicast).

Reverse path forwarding grows into reverse path broadcasting (only the parent router of each network forwards onto it) and reverse path multicasting (routers with no members downstream send prune messages, and graft messages rejoin the tree).
Dense-mode protocols (DVMRP, PIM-DM) flood first and prune later; sparse-mode protocols (PIM-SM, CBT) send nothing until a receiver explicitly joins through the rendezvous point or core.
PIM-SM starts on a shared tree (*, G) rooted at the rendezvous point and can switch to a source tree (S, G) once traffic flows.

224.0.0.0/24 is link-local and never forwarded (224.0.0.1 all hosts, 224.0.0.2 all routers); 232.0.0.0/8 is for source-specific multicast and 239.0.0.0/8 is administratively scoped, like private addresses.
On Ethernet the low 23 bits of the group address are copied into 01-00-5E-00-00-00, so 32 IPv4 groups share each multicast MAC address and hosts must still filter by IP address.

concepts.text: Common mistakes: RIP's 15 hops is a metric limit (16 means unreachable), not the IP TTL. OSPF runs directly over IP as protocol 89, not over TCP or UDP, while BGP needs TCP port 179. Administrative distance only chooses between different sources offering the same prefix: the longest matching prefix always wins first, and metrics of different protocols are never compared. IGMP is not a multicast routing protocol; it only tells the local router which groups have members, and PIM, DVMRP or MOSPF build the trees.

formulas.plainText: Path cost = sum of link costs along the path

notes.text: Transport of routing protocols is a favourite detail: RIP uses UDP 520, OSPF sits directly on IP as protocol 89, BGP uses TCP 179. OSPF backbone is always area 0.
RIP's 16 = infinity limit is a design choice that bounds count-to-infinity: the larger infinity is, the longer bad news takes to spread, so RIP trades network diameter for convergence time.
Do not call BGP a distance vector or link state protocol. It is a path vector protocol: it advertises whole AS paths and chooses routes by policy, not by the smallest metric.

formulas.title: OSPF interface cost
formulas.description: Default OSPF metric with a 100 Mbps reference bandwidth: 10 Mbps gives 10, 100 Mbps gives 1.

formulas.title: Path metric
formulas.plainText: C_path = sum of c_i over the links
formulas.description: RIP adds 1 per hop and OSPF adds interface costs; the path with the smallest total is installed.

formulas.title: RIP infinity
formulas.description: A RIP route with metric 16 is unreachable, which limits RIP networks to a 15-hop diameter.

flashcards.front: What are the transport details of RIP, OSPF and BGP?
flashcards.back: RIP runs over UDP port 520, OSPF directly over IP as protocol 89, and BGP over TCP port 179.

flashcards.front: How does BGP prevent routing loops?
flashcards.back: Each route carries an AS_PATH listing every AS it has passed through; a router discards any advertisement whose AS_PATH already contains its own AS number.

flashcards.front: What is reverse path forwarding in multicast routing?
flashcards.back: A router forwards a multicast packet only if it arrived on the interface on its own shortest path back to the source; packets arriving elsewhere are dropped.

questions.questionText: BGP peers exchange routing information over which transport?
options: UDP port 520
TCP port 179
IP protocol 89
UDP port 179
questions.explanation: BGP uses TCP port 179 so that its incremental updates are delivered reliably. UDP 520 is RIP and IP protocol 89 is OSPF.

questions.questionText: In IPv4 multicasting, which protocol manages group membership between hosts and their local multicast router?
options: IGMP (Internet Group Management Protocol)
BGP (Border Gateway Protocol)
RARP (Reverse Address Resolution Protocol)
ICMP (Internet Control Message Protocol)
questions.explanation: Hosts use IGMP (IP protocol 2) to report which multicast groups they want, and the local router uses IGMP queries to learn which groups have members on each interface. Routers then build the distribution trees among themselves with a multicast routing protocol such as PIM.

questions.questionText: Which pair lists only interior gateway protocols (IGPs)?
options: OSPF and BGP
RIP and BGP
RIP and OSPF
BGP and IS-IS
questions.explanation: RIP and OSPF route inside one autonomous system. BGP is the exterior gateway protocol used between autonomous systems, so every pair containing BGP is wrong.

questions.questionText: What is an autonomous system (AS) in Internet routing?
options: A single LAN segment connected through one switch
A group of networks and routers under one administrative authority with a common routing policy, identified by an AS number
A set of routers that all come from the same vendor
Any network that assigns its own host addresses with DHCP
questions.explanation: An AS, such as an ISP or a large organisation, runs its own interior routing and has a registered AS number (16-bit originally, now 32-bit) that BGP uses. It is defined by administration and policy, not by the LAN technology or equipment vendor.

questions.questionText: In RIP, what does a route with a metric of 16 mean?
options: The destination is 16 hops away and the route is valid
The route is the default route
The route has the highest priority in the table
The destination is unreachable, because 16 is RIP's value for infinity
questions.explanation: RIP allows hop counts from 1 to 15; a metric of 16 is infinity and marks the destination unreachable. This small infinity limits count-to-infinity loops but also limits a RIP network's diameter to 15 hops.

questions.questionText: A RIP router using the RFC 2453 default timers stops hearing any update for a route at time t = 0. When is the route marked unreachable (metric 16), and when is it deleted from the table?
options: Marked unreachable at 180 s, and deleted at 300 s when the 120 s garbage-collection timer expires
Marked unreachable at 30 s, and deleted at 60 s
Marked unreachable at 90 s, and deleted at 180 s
Marked unreachable at 120 s, and deleted at 300 s when a 180 s timer expires
questions.explanation: The timeout is 180 s (six missed 30 s updates); the route is then advertised with metric 16 while the 120 s garbage-collection timer runs, so it is removed at 180 + 120 = 300 s. Swapping the two timers gives the wrong 120 s figure.

questions.questionText: Which feature does RIPv2 add over RIPv1?
options: Routes are computed with Dijkstra's algorithm from flooded link states
The maximum hop count is raised from 15 to 255
Each route entry carries its subnet mask (supporting VLSM and CIDR), updates go to the multicast address 224.0.0.9, and authentication is possible
Updates are carried over TCP port 520 for reliable delivery
questions.explanation: RIPv1 is classful, broadcasts its updates and has no authentication; RIPv2 is classless, multicasts to 224.0.0.9 and supports authentication. Both remain distance vector protocols over UDP port 520 with the same 15-hop limit.

questions.questionText: In a multi-area OSPF network, every area must connect to which area, called the backbone?
options: Area 1
Area 255
Whichever area has the most routers
questions.explanation: The backbone is area 0, written 0.0.0.0; traffic between two areas always passes through it by way of area border routers, which keeps inter-area routing loop-free. An area without a direct link to area 0 must reach it through a virtual link across another area.

questions.questionText: Router R running RIP has the entries N1 = 4 hops via X, N2 = 2 hops via Y and N3 = 6 hops via Z. It receives an update from neighbour Y advertising N1 = 3, N2 = 5, N3 = 5 and N4 = 14. Following the RFC 2453 rules (each hop adds 1), what are R's entries for N2 and N4 afterwards?
options: N2 = 2 hops via Y (unchanged), and N4 = 15 hops via Y
N2 = 6 hops via Y, and N4 is not added because it is unreachable
N2 = 5 hops via Y, and N4 = 14 hops via Y
N2 = 6 hops via Y, and N4 = 15 hops via Y
questions.explanation: Y is R's current next hop for N2, so R must accept Y's worse news: 5 + 1 = 6 via Y. N4 is new and 14 + 1 = 15 is still below infinity (16), so it is added via Y; N1 (4 via Y equals 4 via X) and N3 (6 via Y equals 6 via Z) are not better and stay unchanged.

questions.questionText: OSPF gives each outgoing interface the cost 10^8 / bandwidth (in bps), dropping any fractional part. A path crosses a 10 Mbps Ethernet link, a 1.544 Mbps T1 link and a 100 Mbps Fast Ethernet link. What is the total OSPF cost of the path?
questions.explanation: Costs are 10^8/10^7 = 10, 10^8/(1.544 × 10^6) = 64.77, which becomes 64, and 10^8/10^8 = 1, so the path costs 10 + 64 + 1 = 75. Rounding the T1 up gives 76, a 10^9 reference gives 757, and 3 is just the hop count.

questions.questionText: Path P1 crosses three 10 Gbps links; path P2 crosses one 1 Gbps link and one 100 Mbps link. OSPF cost per link is reference / bandwidth with the fraction dropped and a minimum of 1. Which path does OSPF prefer with the old default reference of 100 Mbps, and which with the reference raised to 100 Gbps?
options: P1 in both cases, because it uses the fastest links
P2 with the 100 Mbps reference (cost 2 against 3); P1 with the 100 Gbps reference (cost 30 against 1100)
P2 in both cases, because it crosses fewer links
P1 with the 100 Mbps reference (cost 3 against 2); P2 with the 100 Gbps reference (cost 1100 against 30)
questions.explanation: With 10^8 every link of 100 Mbps or faster costs 1, so P1 = 3 and P2 = 2 and OSPF wrongly prefers the slower P2. With 10^11 the costs are 10 per 10 Gbps link (P1 = 30) and 100 + 1000 = 1100 for P2, so OSPF correctly prefers P1; OSPF always picks the lower total cost.

questions.questionText: Which OSPF router has interfaces in the backbone and in at least one other area, and summarises routes between them?
options: Autonomous system boundary router (ASBR)
Designated router (DR)
Area border router (ABR)
Internal router
questions.explanation: An ABR has interfaces in area 0 and in at least one other area and sends type 3 summary LSAs between them. An ASBR instead imports routes from outside OSPF, and a DR serves one multi-access segment.

questions.questionText: How is the designated router (DR) elected on an OSPF broadcast network?
options: The lowest priority value wins, and a tie is broken by the lowest router ID
The router with the fastest interface always wins
The router with the most neighbours in the area wins
The highest interface priority wins, a tie is broken by the highest router ID, and a router with priority 0 can never become DR
questions.explanation: OSPF priority ranges from 0 to 255 with a default of 1; the highest priority becomes DR, the next highest BDR, and the highest router ID breaks ties. Priority 0 removes a router from the election.

questions.questionText: Ten OSPF routers share one Ethernet segment. How many adjacencies would be needed if every pair formed one, and how many are formed when a DR and a BDR are elected?
options: 45 without a DR, and 9 with a DR and BDR
45 without a DR, and 17 with a DR and BDR
90 without a DR, and 17 with a DR and BDR
45 without a DR, and 18 with a DR and BDR
questions.explanation: A full mesh needs n(n − 1)/2 = 10 × 9/2 = 45 adjacencies. With a DR and BDR each of the 8 DROthers forms two adjacencies (16) and the DR and BDR form one with each other, giving 2n − 3 = 17; 18 counts the DR–BDR adjacency twice.

questions.questionText: Which OSPF LSA is originated by the designated router to describe a multi-access network and all the routers attached to it?
options: Type 2, network LSA
Type 1, router LSA
Type 3, summary LSA
Type 5, AS-external LSA
questions.explanation: The DR originates the type 2 network LSA listing every router on the segment. Every router originates its own type 1 router LSA, ABRs send type 3 summary LSAs, and ASBRs send type 5 external LSAs.

questions.questionText: Which OSPF packet type discovers neighbours and keeps adjacencies alive, sent every 10 seconds by default on broadcast links?
options: Database Description
Link State Request
Hello
Link State Acknowledgement
questions.explanation: Hello packets find neighbours, check that parameters such as area ID and timers match, and elect the DR; a neighbour silent for the dead interval (40 s by default) is declared down. The other packet types synchronise and acknowledge the link state database.

questions.questionText: On an Ethernet segment, an OSPF router that is neither the DR nor the BDR detects a change on one of its links. To which destination address does it send its Link State Update?
options: 224.0.0.5, the AllSPFRouters address
224.0.0.9, the RIPv2 routers address
255.255.255.255, the limited broadcast address
224.0.0.6, the AllDRouters address
questions.explanation: A DROther sends updates to 224.0.0.6 so that only the DR and BDR receive them; the DR then floods the change to every OSPF router on the segment at 224.0.0.5. 224.0.0.9 belongs to RIPv2.

questions.questionText: Which statement correctly distinguishes eBGP from iBGP?
options: eBGP sessions run between routers in different autonomous systems; iBGP sessions run between routers of the same AS to share the routes learned from outside
eBGP is the encrypted version of BGP, while iBGP sends updates in plain text
eBGP runs over TCP, while iBGP runs over UDP
iBGP connects an organisation to its ISP, while eBGP is used only inside the organisation
questions.explanation: External BGP exchanges routes across an AS boundary, and internal BGP carries those routes to the other BGP routers of the same AS. Both use TCP port 179; the e and i refer to where the peer is, not to encryption.

questions.questionText: A BGP router in AS 65010 receives an UPDATE from an eBGP peer for 198.51.100.0/24 with the AS_PATH 65020 65030 65010 65040. What does the router do?
options: It accepts the route, because it is the only one it has for this prefix
It discards the route, because its own AS number already appears in the AS_PATH, which shows a loop
It accepts the route after removing 65010 from the AS_PATH
It passes the route unchanged to its iBGP peers but does not use it itself
questions.explanation: Path vector loop prevention: a route whose AS_PATH already contains the receiver's own AS number has passed through that AS before, so accepting it would create a loop. The route is ignored whatever other routes exist.

questions.questionText: A BGP router in AS 65001 learns three routes to the same prefix. R1: AS_PATH 65002 65009, LOCAL_PREF 100. R2: AS_PATH 65003 65001 65009, LOCAL_PREF 300. R3: AS_PATH 65004 65007 65008 65009, LOCAL_PREF 200. All other attributes are equal and no vendor-specific weight is set. Which route becomes the best path?
options: R1, because it has the shortest AS_PATH
R2, because it has the highest LOCAL_PREF
R3
None, because one of the paths contains a loop
questions.explanation: R2 contains the router's own AS 65001, so it is discarded as a loop before selection. Between R1 and R3, the higher LOCAL_PREF (200) is compared before AS_PATH length, so R3 wins even though its AS_PATH is longer.

questions.questionText: Which BGP message is exchanged periodically to confirm that a peer is still alive when there are no routing changes to send?
options: OPEN
UPDATE
NOTIFICATION
KEEPALIVE
questions.explanation: KEEPALIVE messages, usually sent every third of the hold time, stop the hold timer from expiring. OPEN starts a session, UPDATE carries route changes and NOTIFICATION reports an error and closes the session.

questions.questionText: An AS has 8 routers running iBGP with no route reflectors or confederations. Because a route learned from an iBGP peer is never passed on to another iBGP peer, the routers must be fully meshed. How many iBGP sessions are needed?
questions.explanation: Each pair of routers needs one TCP session: n(n − 1)/2 = 8 × 7/2 = 28. 56 counts every session twice, and 7 is only the sessions of one router; route reflectors exist to avoid this quadratic growth.

questions.questionText: Why is BGP called a path vector protocol?
options: It floods link state advertisements and runs Dijkstra's algorithm on them
It advertises only a hop count for each destination
Each route it advertises carries the list of autonomous systems (the AS_PATH) that the route passes through
It sends each packet along every possible path at once
questions.explanation: Instead of a single distance, a BGP route carries the full sequence of AS numbers to the destination. This lets routers detect loops and apply policy to whole paths; flooding link states is link state routing and hop counts are RIP.

questions.questionText: On a Cisco router with the default administrative distances, the prefix 172.20.0.0/16 is learned from RIP with a metric of 3 hops and from OSPF with a cost of 200. Which route is installed in the routing table?
options: The RIP route, because a metric of 3 is lower than 200
The OSPF route, because OSPF's administrative distance (110) is lower than RIP's (120)
Both routes, with traffic shared equally between them
The RIP route, because RIP's administrative distance is lower than OSPF's
questions.explanation: Metrics of different protocols are not comparable, so the router picks the source with the lower administrative distance: OSPF 110 beats RIP 120. The metric only chooses between routes learned from the same protocol.

questions.questionText: A Cisco router with default administrative distances has three routes: a static route 10.1.0.0/16 via R1, a RIP route 10.1.1.0/24 via R2 and an OSPF route 10.1.0.0/16 via R3. Which next hops are used for packets to 10.1.1.9 and to 10.1.2.9?
options: Both via R1, because the static route has the lowest administrative distance
questions.explanation: For the /16 the static route (distance 1) beats OSPF (110), so the table holds 10.1.0.0/16 via R1 and 10.1.1.0/24 via R2. Forwarding then uses the longest matching prefix: 10.1.1.9 matches the /24 (R2), while 10.1.2.9 matches only the /16 (R1).

questions.questionText: Router R's unicast route back to multicast source S leaves through interface e1. A multicast packet from S arrives on interface e2. What does R do under reverse path forwarding?
options: It forwards the packet on all interfaces except e2
It forwards the packet only on e1, back towards S
It discards the packet, because it did not arrive on the interface R itself uses to reach S
It sends the packet to the rendezvous point to be forwarded again
questions.explanation: The RPF check accepts a multicast packet only if it arrives on the interface of the router's shortest path back to the source; copies arriving elsewhere are duplicates or looping and are dropped. A packet that passes the check is forwarded on the other interfaces of the tree.

questions.questionText: A multicast group has a few members scattered across a large network. Which multicast routing protocol suits it best, building trees only through explicit joins towards a rendezvous point?
options: PIM-SM (PIM sparse mode)
PIM-DM (PIM dense mode)
DVMRP
MOSPF
questions.explanation: PIM-SM sends traffic only where receivers have joined through the rendezvous point, which avoids flooding a large network. PIM-DM and DVMRP flood and prune, which suits groups with members almost everywhere, and MOSPF floods membership information to every router.

questions.questionText: Which multicast routing protocol adds group-membership LSAs to a link state unicast protocol so that every router can compute source-based trees with Dijkstra's algorithm?
options: DVMRP
PIM-SM
IGMPv3
MOSPF (Multicast OSPF)
questions.explanation: MOSPF extends OSPF with group-membership LSAs; each router then computes a shortest-path tree rooted at the source for each group. DVMRP is distance vector with flood-and-prune, PIM-SM uses a rendezvous point, and IGMPv3 is a host membership protocol.

questions.questionText: Which statement about IGMP is correct?
options: It runs between routers in different autonomous systems to exchange multicast routes
It runs between hosts and the multicast routers on their own network, with messages sent at TTL 1, and IGMPv2 added an explicit Leave Group message
It is carried over TCP port 179
It builds the multicast distribution tree across the whole Internet, so PIM is not needed
questions.explanation: IGMP (IP protocol 2) is a local host-to-router membership protocol and never leaves the network, which is why it uses TTL 1. IGMPv2 added Leave Group so routers stop forwarding sooner; multicast routing protocols such as PIM build the trees between routers.

questions.questionText: Routers R1–R4 have links R1–R2 cost 1, R1–R3 cost 3, R2–R3 cost 1, R2–R4 cost 4 and R3–R4 cost 1 (the same in both directions), and multicast source S is attached to R1. Using reverse path forwarding on the unicast shortest paths, from which neighbour does R3 accept S's packets, and from which does R4 accept them?
options: R3 accepts them from R2, and R4 accepts them from R3
R3 accepts them from R1, and R4 accepts them from R2
R3 accepts them from R1, and R4 accepts them from R3
R3 accepts them from R2, and R4 accepts them from R2
questions.explanation: R3's shortest path to R1 is R3–R2–R1 (cost 2, against 3 on the direct link), so R3 accepts only copies from R2 and drops those from R1. R4's shortest path is R4–R3–R2–R1 (cost 3, against 4 via R3–R1 and 5 via R2), so R4 accepts only copies from R3.

questions.questionText: Which statement about RIP, OSPF and BGP is NOT correct?
options: RIP and OSPF are interior gateway protocols, while BGP is used between autonomous systems
BGP chooses routes by policy and path attributes, not just by distance
OSPF, like RIP, cannot be used on paths longer than 15 hops
RIP suits small networks because it is simple, but it converges slowly
questions.explanation: The 15-hop limit belongs to RIP alone; OSPF uses bandwidth-based costs with no hop-count limit, which is one reason it suits large networks. The other three statements are correct.

concepts.text: IP: Connectionless Datagram Delivery

The Internet Protocol (IP) is the network-layer protocol of the TCP/IP suite. It is connectionless and unreliable (best effort): each datagram is routed independently, and datagrams may be lost, duplicated, delayed or delivered out of order without IP noticing. Reliability, if needed, is added by TCP above it, while ICMP reports errors. An IPv4 datagram has a header of 20 to 60 bytes followed by data; the total datagram size can be up to 65,535 bytes.
IPv4 Datagram Header

concepts.text: Fragmentation and Reassembly

Each link has a maximum transfer unit (MTU), 1500 bytes for Ethernet. A router that must send a datagram larger than the next link's MTU splits it into fragments, each with its own IP header copied from the original, unless DF is set, in which case it drops the datagram and returns an ICMP error. All fragments share the identification value; MF = 1 on all but the last; the offset gives each fragment's data position in 8-byte units, so every fragment except the last carries a multiple of 8 data bytes. Reassembly happens only at the destination host.

concepts.plainText: Offset field = position of first data byte / 8

concepts.text: Working through the fragmentation example and related header fields:
items: The 4000-byte datagram has a 20-byte header, so 3980 data bytes must be carried.
Maximum data per fragment = 1500 − 20 = 1480 bytes, already a multiple of 8, giving 1480 + 1480 + 1020 bytes.
TTL prevents datagrams looping forever: common starting values are 64 or 128, and a router sends ICMP Time Exceeded when TTL reaches 0.
The protocol field tells the receiver which module gets the payload: 1 ICMP, 2 IGMP, 6 TCP, 17 UDP, 41 IPv6-in-IPv4, 89 OSPF.

concepts.text: ARP, RARP, BOOTP and DHCP
Address resolution maps between logical (IP) and physical (MAC) addresses:
items: ARP maps a known IP address to a MAC address: the sender broadcasts an ARP request ('who has 192.168.1.1?') and the owner replies by unicast; results are cached in the ARP table. EtherType 0x0806.
Proxy ARP lets a router answer on behalf of hosts on another network; gratuitous ARP announces one's own mapping and detects duplicate addresses.
RARP does the reverse, MAC to IP, for diskless machines at boot; it needs a RARP server on every physical network and returns only an IP address.
BOOTP (UDP 67 server, 68 client) replaced RARP: it runs above IP, can cross routers via relay agents and also supplies mask, gateway and boot file, but uses static tables.
DHCP extends BOOTP with dynamic, leased allocation from a pool (Discover, Offer, Request, Acknowledge) and is the standard method today.

concepts.text: ICMP: Error Reporting and Diagnostics

rows: Network, host, port unreachable; fragmentation needed but DF set
Router tells host a better next-hop router

concepts.text: ICMP messages are carried inside IP datagrams (protocol 1) and drive two everyday tools:
items: ping sends ICMP Echo Request (type 8) and waits for Echo Reply (type 0), reporting reachability, round-trip time and packet loss.

traceroute (tracert on Windows) sends probes with TTL = 1, 2, 3, …; each router where TTL expires returns Time Exceeded (type 11), revealing the path hop by hop. The destination answers with Port Unreachable (UDP probes, Unix) or Echo Reply (ICMP probes, Windows).
ICMP never reports errors about ICMP error messages, about fragments other than the first, or about broadcast/multicast datagrams, to avoid message storms.
An ICMP error carries the original IP header plus the first 8 bytes of its data so the sender can identify the affected connection.

concepts.text: Going Deeper: IP, ICMP, RARP and DHCP

In four words IP is connectionless, unreliable, best-effort and routed: nothing is set up before sending, delivery is not guaranteed, nothing is retransmitted, and every datagram is routed on its own by its destination address. ICMP is IP's companion for error reporting and diagnostics; the ping command uses its Echo Request and Echo Reply to test connectivity, and traceroute uses Time Exceeded messages to find the path. ARP turns a known IP address into a MAC address, while RARP did the reverse (MAC to IP) and has been replaced by DHCP.

Worked example 1: 2400-byte datagram (20-byte header, 2380 data bytes), next link MTU 1000
Data per fragment = 1000 - 20 = 980 -> round down to a multiple of 8 -> 976
Frag  Data bytes    Offset field      MF  Total length
1     0-975         0/8    = 0        1   996
2     976-1951      976/8  = 122      1   996
3     1952-2379     1952/8 = 244      0   448
A later link has MTU 500, so fragment 2 is split again (480 data bytes per piece):
2a    976-1455      976/8  = 122      1   500
2b    1456-1935     1456/8 = 182      1   500
2c    1936-1951     1936/8 = 242      1   36
Offsets stay relative to the original datagram, and 2c keeps MF = 1
because fragment 3 still follows; only the true end of the data has MF = 0

concepts.plainText: Data per fragment d = 8 × floor((MTU − H) / 8); number of fragments N = ceil(D / d), where H is the header length and D the original data length

concepts.text: The field sizes fit together: the 13-bit offset counts 8-byte blocks, so it can reach 2^13 × 8 = 65,536 bytes, just enough for the largest datagram of 65,535 bytes allowed by the 16-bit Total Length. Every router must recompute the header checksum because it decrements the TTL, which is also why the checksum covers only the header; checking the whole payload at every hop would be slow and is left to TCP, UDP and the link layer. Fragments are reassembled only at the destination because they may travel by different routes. If any one fragment is lost, the reassembly timer expires and the whole datagram is discarded, so fragmentation multiplies the effect of packet loss.

Worked example 2: IPv4 header checksum (a ping from 192.168.1.10 to 8.8.8.8)
Header words: 4500 0054 1A2B 4000 4001 [0000] C0A8 010A 0808 0808
Sum = 4500 + 0054 + 1A2B + 4000 + 4001 + C0A8 + 010A + 0808 + 0808 = 1B142
Fold the carry back in: B142 + 1 = B143
Checksum = one's complement of B143 = 4EBC, so the header carries 40 01 4E BC
Receiver: sum of all ten words including 4EBC = B143 + 4EBC = FFFF -> no error found
Next router: TTL 64 -> 63 turns word 4001 into 3F01, so it recomputes the checksum: 4FBC

rows: A router with no route to the network
The last router, when the host does not answer ARP
The destination host, with no handler for the Protocol value
The destination host, with no process on the UDP port
A router; it includes the next-hop MTU for path MTU discovery
A router or firewall that filters the packet

concepts.text:
Worked trace: traceroute (Unix: UDP probes to port 33434 and up, 3 per TTL), target 4 hops away
TTL 1 -> R1 decrements it to 0, drops the probe, returns Time Exceeded (11/0) -> line 1: R1
TTL 2 -> R2 returns Time Exceeded -> line 2: R2
TTL 3 -> R3 returns Time Exceeded -> line 3: R3
TTL 4 -> target: no process on that UDP port -> Port Unreachable (3/3) -> trace ends
Each line shows three round-trip times; '* * *' means no answer before the timeout
Windows tracert sends ICMP Echo Requests instead and stops at the Echo Reply (type 0)
ping: Echo Request (8/0) carries an identifier and sequence number; the reply echoes them
A reply arriving with TTL 57 from a host that starts at 64 has crossed 64 - 57 = 7 routers
DHCP step by step (Discover, Offer, Request, Acknowledge, remembered as DORA):
items: Discover: the client, still without an address, broadcasts from 0.0.0.0, UDP port 68, to 255.255.255.255, UDP port 67.
Offer: each server that can help offers an address with mask, default gateway, DNS servers and a lease time.
Request: the client broadcasts which offer it accepts, which also tells the other servers that their offers were declined.
Acknowledge: the chosen server confirms the lease. A client that finds the address already in use (for example by an ARP probe) sends DHCPDECLINE, and a server can refuse a request with DHCPNAK.

Renewal: at T1 (50 % of the lease by default) the client unicasts a Request to its own server; if that fails, at T2 (87.5 %) it broadcasts to any server (rebinding). DHCPRELEASE returns the address early.

A relay agent on the router turns the client's broadcast into a unicast to a server on another subnet and writes its own interface address into the giaddr field, so the server picks the right address pool.

rows: No: a server is needed on every network
IP address, mask, default gateway, DNS server, boot file
All of BOOTP's plus a lease time and many more options
Dynamic leases from a pool, or fixed reservations

concepts.text: Fragmentation checklist: subtract the header from the MTU and round the data down to a multiple of 8; offset field = data bytes before this fragment / 8; Total Length = data + header; every fragment keeps the original Identification; MF = 1 on every fragment except the one holding the last byte of the original data. To find the original size from the last fragment, compute offset × 8 + (Total Length − header) and add one header.

Common mistakes: the fragment offset is in 8-byte units and HLEN in 4-byte words, but Total Length is in bytes and includes the header. The header checksum covers the header only; TCP and UDP checksums cover the data. TTL is decremented by one per router, so it acts as a hop limit rather than a time. A failed ping does not prove a host is down, because many hosts and firewalls block ICMP Echo. ICMP travels inside IP (protocol 1) but is still a network-layer protocol.

notes.text: Fragmentation questions: subtract the header from the MTU, round data down to a multiple of 8, then divide byte positions by 8 for the offset field. 4000-byte datagram over MTU 1500 gives offsets 0, 185, 370.

The IPv4 header checksum covers only the header, not the data, and must be recomputed at every router because TTL changes. HLEN and fragment offset are both scaled fields: multiply HLEN by 4 and the offset by 8.
ICMP is a network-layer protocol even though it is carried inside IP datagrams, just as ARP is usually drawn at the boundary of the data link and network layers.

formulas.title: IPv4 header length
formulas.description: HLEN counts 4-byte words, so 5 means a 20-byte header and 15 means the maximum 60 bytes.

formulas.title: Fragment offset
formulas.description: The 13-bit offset field is measured in 8-byte units, so a fragment starting at data byte 2960 has offset 370.

formulas.title: Data per fragment
formulas.description: The largest data size per non-final fragment; for MTU 1500 and a 20-byte header it is 1480 bytes.

flashcards.front: How does traceroute discover the routers on a path?
flashcards.back: It sends probes with TTL 1, 2, 3, …; each router where the TTL reaches 0 returns ICMP Time Exceeded (type 11), revealing its address and the round-trip time.

flashcards.front: Why did BOOTP and DHCP replace RARP?
flashcards.back: RARP works only at the data link level, needs a server on every network and returns only an IP address; BOOTP/DHCP run over UDP, cross routers via relays and supply mask, gateway and DNS, and DHCP leases addresses dynamically.

flashcards.front: Which IPv4 header fields are used in fragmentation?
flashcards.back: Identification (same for all fragments), flags DF and MF, and the 13-bit fragment offset measured in 8-byte units.

questions.questionText: A 4000-byte IPv4 datagram with a 20-byte header is sent over a link with an MTU of 1500 bytes. What is the fragment offset field value of the third fragment?
questions.explanation: Each fragment carries at most 1480 data bytes, so the third fragment starts at data byte 2960; the offset field is in 8-byte units, giving 2960/8 = 370.

questions.questionText: The HLEN field of an IPv4 datagram contains the value 15. What is the length of the header?
options: 60 bytes
15 bytes
30 bytes
120 bytes
questions.explanation: HLEN counts 32-bit (4-byte) words, so 15 × 4 = 60 bytes, the maximum IPv4 header size including 40 bytes of options.

questions.questionText: The traceroute utility identifies intermediate routers mainly through which ICMP message?
options: Echo reply (type 0)
Redirect (type 5)
Source quench (type 4)
Time exceeded (type 11)
questions.explanation: traceroute sends probes with increasing TTL; each router that decrements TTL to zero discards the probe and returns Time Exceeded, identifying itself.

questions.questionText: What does 'best-effort delivery' mean for IP?
options: IP retransmits every lost datagram until the receiver acknowledges it
IP tries to deliver every datagram but gives no guarantee: datagrams may be lost, duplicated, delayed or delivered out of order without any notice
IP reserves bandwidth along the path for each connection before sending
IP always delivers datagrams in order, although sometimes with extra delay
questions.explanation: IP is connectionless and unreliable: it keeps no connection state, sends no acknowledgements and does no retransmission. Reliability and ordering, when needed, are added by TCP above it.

questions.questionText: Which ICMP messages does the ping command use?
options: Time Exceeded (type 11) and Echo Reply (type 0)
Router Solicitation (type 10) and Router Advertisement (type 9)
Destination Unreachable (type 3) and Redirect (type 5)
Echo Request (type 8) and Echo Reply (type 0)
questions.explanation: ping sends Echo Requests and measures the time until the matching Echo Reply returns, reporting reachability, round-trip time and loss. Time Exceeded is the message that traceroute relies on.

questions.questionText: How are ICMP messages carried across a network?
options: Inside IP datagrams, with the Protocol field set to 1
Inside UDP datagrams sent to port 7
Directly in Ethernet frames with EtherType 0x0806
Inside TCP segments sent to port 1
questions.explanation: ICMP messages are encapsulated in IP datagrams with Protocol = 1, yet ICMP is still counted as a network-layer protocol because it serves IP itself. EtherType 0x0806 identifies ARP.

questions.questionText: What is the purpose of the Time to Live (TTL) field in an IPv4 header?
options: To tell the destination how long to keep the datagram in its buffer
To set how long the source waits for an acknowledgement before retransmitting
To stop a datagram from circulating forever, for example in a routing loop: each router decrements it and discards the datagram when it reaches 0
To record the time at which the datagram was sent so that delay can be measured
questions.explanation: Every router decrements TTL by at least 1, so in practice it is a hop limit; when it reaches 0 the router drops the datagram and sends ICMP Time Exceeded to the source. IP has no acknowledgements or timestamps in this field.

questions.questionText: Which pairing of IPv4 Protocol field value and payload is correct?
options: 6 – UDP
1 – ICMP
17 – TCP
2 – OSPF
questions.explanation: The Protocol field names the payload: 1 ICMP, 2 IGMP, 6 TCP, 17 UDP and 89 OSPF. The distractors swap TCP and UDP or give IGMP's number to OSPF.

questions.questionText: How does the destination know which IPv4 fragments belong to the same original datagram?
options: They all carry the same fragment offset
They all carry the same Total Length
They all carry the same header checksum
They all carry the same Identification value, together with the same source address, destination address and protocol
questions.explanation: The source gives each datagram an Identification number, and every fragment copies it; the receiver groups fragments by Identification, source, destination and protocol. Offsets, lengths and checksums differ from fragment to fragment.

questions.questionText: What is the correct order of DHCP messages when a client obtains an address for the first time?
options: Discover, Offer, Request, Acknowledge
Request, Offer, Discover, Acknowledge
Discover, Request, Offer, Acknowledge
Offer, Discover, Acknowledge, Request
questions.explanation: The client broadcasts a Discover, servers answer with Offers, the client Requests one offer and the chosen server confirms it with an Acknowledge (DORA).

questions.questionText: A UDP datagram reaches its destination host, but no process is listening on the destination port. What does the host send back?
options: ICMP Destination Unreachable with code 1 (host unreachable)
ICMP Time Exceeded
ICMP Destination Unreachable with code 3 (port unreachable)
ICMP Redirect
questions.explanation: The host itself is reachable, so it answers with type 3 code 3, port unreachable; host unreachable (code 1) comes from a router that cannot reach the host. Unix traceroute uses exactly this reply to recognise the destination.

questions.questionText: An IPv4 datagram has Total Length = 1500 and HLEN = 6. How many bytes of data (payload) does it carry?
questions.explanation: HLEN counts 4-byte words, so the header is 6 × 4 = 24 bytes and the payload is 1500 − 24 = 1476 bytes. Subtracting 6 gives 1494, and 1480 wrongly assumes a 20-byte header.

questions.questionText: An IPv4 header carries 10 bytes of options. What value goes into the HLEN field, and how much padding is needed?
options: HLEN = 30, with no padding
HLEN = 8, with 2 bytes of padding
HLEN = 7, with 2 bytes of padding
HLEN = 10, with 2 bytes of padding
questions.explanation: 20 + 10 = 30 bytes is not a multiple of 4, so 2 padding bytes bring the header to 32 bytes, and HLEN = 32/4 = 8. HLEN counts 4-byte words, never bytes.

questions.questionText: A 3000-byte IPv4 datagram with a 20-byte header must cross a link with an MTU of 1400 bytes. What is the Total Length field of the last fragment?
options: 240 bytes
228 bytes
200 bytes
248 bytes
questions.explanation: Data per fragment = 1400 − 20 = 1380, rounded down to a multiple of 8 = 1376; 2980 − 2 × 1376 = 228 data bytes remain, so the last fragment's Total Length is 228 + 20 = 248. Not rounding to 8 gives 240, and forgetting the header gives 228.

questions.questionText: An IPv4 fragment arrives with fragment offset 250, MF = 1, Total Length 1020 and HLEN 5. Which bytes of the original data does it carry?
options: Bytes 250 to 1269, and more fragments follow
Bytes 2000 to 3019, and more fragments follow
Bytes 2000 to 2999, and more fragments follow
Bytes 2000 to 2999, and it is the last fragment
questions.explanation: The first data byte is 250 × 8 = 2000 and the fragment carries 1020 − 20 = 1000 data bytes, so it holds bytes 2000–2999. MF = 1 means it is not the last fragment.

questions.questionText: A 1500-byte IPv4 datagram with the DF (don't fragment) bit set reaches a router whose next link has an MTU of 1400 bytes. What does the router do?
options: It drops the datagram and returns ICMP Destination Unreachable, code 4 (fragmentation needed and DF set), giving the next-hop MTU
It fragments the datagram anyway, because the MTU limit overrides DF
It forwards the datagram unchanged and leaves the problem to the next router
It cuts the datagram down to 1400 bytes and clears the DF bit
questions.explanation: With DF = 1 the router may not fragment, so it discards the datagram and reports type 3 code 4 with the MTU of the next link. Path MTU discovery sets DF on purpose and uses these messages to find the largest size that fits the whole path.

questions.questionText: Which statement about the IPv4 header checksum is NOT correct?
options: It is recomputed by every router, because the TTL field changes at each hop
It is the one's complement of the one's complement sum of the header's 16-bit words
A datagram whose header checksum fails is discarded
It covers both the header and the data, so a corrupted payload is also detected
questions.explanation: The IPv4 checksum protects only the header; the data is protected by the TCP or UDP checksum and the link-layer CRC. The other statements are correct.

questions.questionText: With the checksum field set to zero, the one's complement sum of an IPv4 header's 16-bit words (carries already folded back in) is 0x4E2B. What value is placed in the checksum field?
options: 0x4E2B
0xB1D4
0xB1D5
0x2B4E
questions.explanation: The checksum is the one's complement of the sum: every bit of 0x4E2B is inverted, giving 0xFFFF − 0x4E2B = 0xB1D4. 0xB1D5 is the two's complement and 0x4E2B is the uncomplemented sum.

questions.questionText: Host H sends a packet for a remote network to its default router R1. R1's best next hop for that network is router R2, which is on the same LAN as H. What does R1 do?
options: It drops the packet and sends H an ICMP Destination Unreachable
It sends H a Source Quench so that H slows down
It forwards the packet to R2 and sends H an ICMP Redirect (type 5) telling it to use R2 for that destination
It forwards the packet and sends H an ICMP Time Exceeded
questions.explanation: When a packet would leave through the same interface it arrived on, towards a next hop on the sender's own subnet, the router still delivers it but advises the host with a Redirect. The host then sends later packets for that destination straight to R2.

questions.questionText: In which case does a router NOT send an ICMP error message when it discards a datagram?
options: When the discarded datagram itself carries an ICMP error message
When the TTL of an ordinary unicast TCP segment reaches 0
When a datagram with DF set is larger than the next link's MTU
When it has no route to the destination network
questions.explanation: ICMP never reports errors about ICMP error messages, nor about non-first fragments or broadcast and multicast datagrams, so that error messages cannot trigger storms of further errors. The other three cases produce Time Exceeded, Fragmentation Needed and Network Unreachable.

questions.questionText: A ping reply arrives with TTL = 116. The remote host sets an initial TTL of 128, and every router decrements TTL by 1. How many routers did the reply cross?
questions.explanation: Each router lowers the TTL by one, so the number of routers crossed is 128 − 116 = 12. The reply's TTL itself (116) is not a hop count, and adding or dropping one for the end hosts is the usual off-by-one slip.

questions.questionText: ping to a company's web server times out every time, yet the website opens normally in a browser. What is the most likely explanation?
options: The server's IP address has been typed wrongly
The server or a firewall on the path blocks ICMP Echo, while TCP traffic to the web port is allowed
The DNS server cannot be reached
The web server has crashed
questions.explanation: Many hosts and firewalls drop ICMP Echo Requests for security, so ping fails even though TCP connections to port 443 or 80 work. A wrong address, DNS failure or crashed server would also stop the website loading.

questions.questionText: In traceroute output, hop 4 shows '* * *', but hops 5 to 8 answer normally and the trace reaches the destination. What does this mean?
options: The path is broken at hop 4, so hops 5 to 8 are not real
Hop 4 is the destination host, which never answers probes
Router 4 forwards the probes but does not return Time Exceeded messages, for example because ICMP is filtered or rate-limited; the path itself works
Hop 4 is a layer-2 switch, which has no IP address
questions.explanation: Later hops answering proves that packets pass through hop 4; that router simply sends no ICMP reply in time. A switch never appears as a hop at all, because it does not decrement TTL.

questions.questionText: Why was RARP replaced, first by BOOTP and then by DHCP?
options: RARP runs directly over the link layer, so it cannot cross routers and needs a server on every network, and it supplies only an IP address
RARP cannot work with 48-bit MAC addresses
RARP runs over TCP, which made booting too slow
RARP was designed only for IPv6 networks
questions.explanation: A RARP request is a link-layer broadcast (EtherType 0x8035) that routers do not forward, and the reply gives no mask, gateway or DNS server. BOOTP and DHCP run over UDP/IP, cross routers through relay agents and hand out full configuration.

questions.questionText: A client that has no IP address yet sends a DHCPDISCOVER. Which addresses and ports does the datagram use?
options: Source 0.0.0.0, UDP port 67; destination 255.255.255.255, UDP port 68
Source 169.254.0.1, UDP port 68; destination 224.0.0.1, UDP port 67
Source 127.0.0.1, UDP port 68; destination the server's unicast address, UDP port 67
Source 0.0.0.0, UDP port 68; destination 255.255.255.255, UDP port 67
questions.explanation: Without an address the client uses 0.0.0.0 as its source and the limited broadcast 255.255.255.255 as its destination. DHCP servers listen on UDP port 67 and clients on UDP port 68.

questions.questionText: The DHCP server of a company sits on a different subnet from the client PCs. What allows the clients' DHCP broadcasts to reach it?
options: Proxy ARP on the router, which answers the Discover itself
A DHCP relay agent on the router, which forwards each broadcast to the server by unicast and records the client's subnet in the giaddr field
Routers forward the limited broadcast 255.255.255.255 to every subnet
RARP, which carries the request across the router
questions.explanation: Routers never forward 255.255.255.255, so the router's relay agent turns the client broadcast into a unicast to the server's address. The giaddr field tells the server which subnet's address pool to use.

questions.questionText: A DHCP client obtains an 8-hour lease. With the default timer values, when does it first try to renew the lease with its server (T1), and when does it start rebinding with any server (T2)?
options: T1 after 4 hours and T2 after 8 hours
T1 after 2 hours and T2 after 4 hours
T1 after 4 hours and T2 after 7 hours
T1 after 6 hours and T2 after 7.5 hours
questions.explanation: By default T1 = 0.5 × lease = 0.5 × 8 = 4 h and T2 = 0.875 × lease = 0.875 × 8 = 7 h. At 8 h the lease expires and the client must stop using the address.

questions.questionText: The last fragment of an IPv4 datagram arrives with fragment offset 300, MF = 0, Total Length 628 and HLEN 5. The original datagram also had a 20-byte header with no options. What was the Total Length of the original datagram?
options: 3028 bytes
3008 bytes
928 bytes
3048 bytes
questions.explanation: The fragment's data starts at byte 300 × 8 = 2400 and holds 628 − 20 = 608 bytes, so the original data was 2400 + 608 = 3008 bytes; adding one 20-byte header gives 3028. 928 treats the offset as bytes, and 3048 adds a header twice.

questions.questionText: A fragment with offset 185, MF = 1 and Total Length 1500 (20-byte header, 1480 data bytes) reaches a link with an MTU of 620 bytes and is split into three fragments. What are their offset fields and MF bits?
options: Offsets 0, 75 and 150, with MF = 1, 1 and 0
Offsets 185, 260 and 335, with MF = 1, 1 and 0
Offsets 185, 785 and 1385, with MF = 1 in all three
Offsets 185, 260 and 335, with MF = 1 in all three
questions.explanation: Each new fragment carries 620 − 20 = 600 data bytes (a multiple of 8, 75 units), so the offsets are 185, 185 + 75 = 260 and 260 + 75 = 335, still counted from the start of the original datagram. The fragment being split had MF = 1, so more data follows its last piece too and all three keep MF = 1.

questions.questionText: Compute the checksum field of this IPv4 header, given in hexadecimal with the checksum set to zero: 4500 0030 0001 4000 4006 0000 C0A8 0001 C0A8 0002.
questions.explanation: The words add up to 0x2468A; folding the carry gives 0x468A + 0x2 = 0x468C, and its one's complement is 0xB973. 0x468C forgets to complement, 0xB975 drops the carry instead of adding it back, and 0xB974 is the two's complement.

questions.questionText: A router discards a UDP datagram whose TTL has expired (20-byte IPv4 header) and returns ICMP Time Exceeded, including exactly what RFC 792 requires: the original IP header plus the first 8 bytes of its data. The new IPv4 header has no options. What is the Total Length of the datagram carrying the ICMP message?
options: 36 bytes
48 bytes
56 bytes
28 bytes
questions.explanation: Total = new IP header 20 + ICMP header 8 + original IP header 20 + first 8 data bytes = 56 bytes. The quoted 8 bytes hold the UDP ports, which lets the sender find the affected socket; 48 leaves them out and 36 leaves out the original header.

questions.questionText: Unix traceroute sends 3 UDP probes for each TTL value, starting at TTL 1. The destination is behind 5 routers, and every probe is answered. How many probes are sent in total, and which ICMP replies come back?
options: 18 probes; 15 Time Exceeded messages and 3 Port Unreachable messages
15 probes; 15 Time Exceeded messages
18 probes; 18 Time Exceeded messages
6 probes; 5 Time Exceeded messages and 1 Port Unreachable message
questions.explanation: TTL runs from 1 to 6 (5 routers plus the destination), so 6 × 3 = 18 probes are sent. Each of the 5 routers returns 3 Time Exceeded messages (15), and the destination answers its 3 probes with Port Unreachable, which ends the trace.

questions.questionText: Host A pings host B across two routers, R1 and R2, over three Ethernet links, and every ARP cache starts empty. Every device follows RFC 826, so the target of an ARP request also stores the requester's mapping. How many ARP requests are sent in total before A receives the Echo Reply?
questions.explanation: On the way out one request is needed on each link: A for R1, R1 for R2 and R2 for B. Each target learned its requester's MAC from the request, so the reply travels back B to R2 to R1 to A with no further ARP, giving 3 rather than 6.
